_readme: Healthy habits tips and Food facts for the cafeteria menu TVs (CONTRACT Draft 12; cafe-menu.js 1.7.0). Clinical / nutrition content: an item shows ONLY when Dietary has approved it -- "reviewStatus": "approved" together with "reviewedBy" (the reviewer's name) and "reviewedOn" (YYYY-MM-DD). "pending" and "retired" never show. One tip and one fact a day (the New York date picks them, the same on both TVs). No times, no dish names; a tip is never paired with a dish. Where the strip under the menu is short, a fact shows its question and answer without its reveal, and a tip's source moves beside the title (or to the end of the tip): approve each question + answer as a pair that stands on its own. Steps: work/cafe-menu/proof/enhance-1015/MAINTAIN.md section 11.

tips.text: Every meal is a chance to nourish your body. The benefits add up over time, bite by bite.

sources.title: Small Changes Matter. Start Simple with MyPlate Today.
sources.publisher: USDA and HHS, Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020-2025 (dietaryguidelines.gov)
sources.supports: Says healthy eating matters at every stage of life and that the benefits of food choices add up over time, bite by bite.

tips.notes: General encouragement only; no individual instruction. The cited MyPlate sheet belongs to the 2020-2025 Dietary Guidelines edition (the 2025-2030 edition is now current); reviewer to confirm wording still fits.

tips.text: Variety matters: fruits, vegetables, grains, protein foods, and dairy or fortified soy all have a place.

sources.title: Small Changes Matter. Start Simple with MyPlate Today.
sources.publisher: USDA and HHS, Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020-2025 (dietaryguidelines.gov)
sources.supports: States it is important to eat a variety of fruits, vegetables, grains, protein foods, and dairy or fortified soy alternatives.

tips.notes: Names the five MyPlate groups neutrally; no foods are ranked or labelled good/bad. Dietary to confirm the wording suits the current menu and any texture-modified or special diets.

tips.text: Fruits and vegetables fit at any meal or snack. Trying a new one might become a new favorite.

sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025 - 2030 (MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia)
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus, National Library of Medicine (NIH); reviewed 2026-02-09
sources.supports: Has a section encouraging fruits and vegetables throughout the day.

sources.title: Small Changes Matter. Start Simple with MyPlate Today.
sources.publisher: USDA and HHS, Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020-2025 (dietaryguidelines.gov)
sources.supports: Suggests ready-to-eat fruit as a quick snack and trying new vegetables or grains, noting you might discover a new favorite.

tips.notes: Second sentence is an encouragement, not a health claim.

tips.text: Eating regularly can help you feel better and stay focused. Fuel your day one meal at a time.

sources.title: Eating to Boost Energy
sources.publisher: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics (eatright.org); reviewed 2026-04-22
sources.supports: Says people feel better and more focused when they have fuel in their system on a regular basis.

sources.title: How to Practice Intuitive Eating While Supporting Your Nutrition Needs
sources.publisher: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics (eatright.org)
sources.supports: States that regular meals and snacks can help support energy.

tips.notes: The second source sits in the Academy's weight-and-body-positivity section; only the energy statement is used, and the tip contains no weight or body-size message.

tips.text: A snack can bridge the gap between one meal and the next.

sources.title: Eating to Boost Energy
sources.publisher: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics (eatright.org); reviewed 2026-04-22
sources.supports: Describes snacks as a way to bridge from one meal to the next rather than to fill you up.

tips.notes: Reviewer to confirm snack availability on the unit before this is shown.

tips.text: Knowing what's coming can ease mealtime stress. Planning ahead may help.

sources.title: 3 Strategies for Successful Meal Planning
sources.publisher: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics (eatright.org); reviewed 2026-03-03
sources.supports: States that planning ahead may help relieve mealtime stress.

tips.notes: Written for people planning their own meals; here it is a gentle nod to the posted menu. Modest wording (may).

tips.text: Water helps your body keep a normal temperature and cushions your joints.

sources.title: About Water and Healthier Drinks
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Healthy Weight and Growth (page dated 2026-03-05)
sources.supports: Lists keeping a normal temperature and lubricating and cushioning joints among the ways water helps the body.

tips.notes: The CDC page also discusses weight and calories; none of that is used. Reviewer to confirm no patient on a fluid restriction would be confused (the tip is general, not an instruction to drink more).

tips.text: Drinking water can help prevent dehydration, which may cause unclear thinking and mood changes.

sources.title: About Water and Healthier Drinks
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Healthy Weight and Growth (page dated 2026-03-05)
sources.supports: Says drinking water can prevent dehydration, which may cause unclear thinking and mood change, among other effects.

tips.notes: Phrased with can/may as the CDC does. Clinical reviewer to confirm the mood wording is acceptable for this audience; shorter alternative: end the sentence after 'dehydration'.

tips.text: A squeeze of fruit adds a splash of flavor to a glass of water.

sources.title: Small Changes Matter. Start Simple with MyPlate Today.
sources.publisher: USDA and HHS, Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020-2025 (dietaryguidelines.gov)
sources.supports: Suggests chilled plain or sparkling water with a squeeze of fruit for a splash of flavor.

tips.notes: Practical idea only. Show only if citrus or similar is actually available at the water station.

tips.text: People who eat with others more often tend to report feeling happier. Pull up a chair if you like.

sources.title: Breaking Bread: the Functions of Social Eating
sources.publisher: R. I. M. Dunbar, Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology 3(3):198-211, 2017 (PubMed Central)
sources.supports: A national survey found people who eat socially more often feel happier and more satisfied with life and are more engaged with their communities.

tips.notes: Survey (association, not proof of cause; UK adults) so the wording is 'tend to report'. Peer-reviewed. The invitation is optional so patients who prefer quiet are not pressured.

tips.text: Good company can make mealtimes more enjoyable. Share a table whenever it feels right.

sources.title: Health Tips for Older Adults
sources.publisher: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIH)
sources.supports: Advises trying to share meals with someone whose company you enjoy and links good company with more enjoyable meals.

sources.title: Overcoming Roadblocks to Healthy Eating
sources.publisher: National Institute on Aging (NIH)
sources.supports: Suggests cooking or eating with a friend or at a community setting so you have some company while you eat.

tips.notes: Both NIH sources are written for older adults; the tip makes only an enjoyment claim (no nutrition-benefit claim) because adult evidence linking shared meals to diet quality is mixed.

tips.text: Questions about food? Your care team and dietitian are the right people to ask.
tips.source: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics · MedlinePlus (NIH)

sources.title: About RDNs and NDTRs
sources.publisher: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics (eatright.org)
sources.supports: Describes registered dietitian nutritionists as food and nutrition experts who work in hospitals and health care facilities, teaching patients about nutrition.

sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025 - 2030 (MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia)
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus, National Library of Medicine (NIH); reviewed 2026-02-09
sources.supports: Advises discussing dietary changes with a health care provider or registered dietitian.

tips.notes: FACILITY CHECK: Dietary to confirm that patients can reach a dietitian or the care team with food questions, and how, before this is shown.

tips.text: Registered dietitians are food and nutrition experts. Ask your care team how to reach one.

sources.title: About RDNs and NDTRs
sources.publisher: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics (eatright.org)
sources.supports: States that registered dietitian nutritionists are food and nutrition experts with graduate-level education, supervised practice, and a national exam.

tips.notes: FACILITY CHECK: confirm the RCA Greenville process for requesting a dietitian conversation; adjust the second sentence to match.

tips.text: Thinking about changing how you eat? Talk with your care team or dietitian first.

sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025 - 2030 (MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia)
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus, National Library of Medicine (NIH); reviewed 2026-02-09
sources.supports: Says to discuss any dietary changes with your health care provider or registered dietitian first.

tips.notes: A referral, not an instruction about what to eat. Pairs naturally with ffr-12.

facts.question: Roughly how much of an apple is air, which helps it float in water?
facts.reveal: That air is why apples tend to float in water.

sources.title: Apples | SNAP-Ed
sources.publisher: USDA Food and Nutrition Service, SNAP-Ed Connection (Seasonal Produce Guide)
sources.supports: Fun fact: apples are about 25% air and tend to float in water.

facts.question: What is a bunch of bananas called?
facts.reveal: Bananas curve slightly because they grow toward the light.

sources.title: Bananas | SNAP-Ed
sources.publisher: USDA Food and Nutrition Service, SNAP-Ed Connection (Seasonal Produce Guide)
sources.supports: Fun facts: a bunch of bananas is called a hand; bananas curve slightly because they grow toward the light.

facts.question: What do ripe cranberries do when their field is flooded at harvest time?
facts.reveal: That is why cranberry fields are flooded when it is time to harvest.

sources.title: Cranberries | SNAP-Ed
sources.publisher: USDA Food and Nutrition Service, SNAP-Ed Connection (Seasonal Produce Guide)
sources.supports: At harvest the fields are flooded and the cranberries float to the top of the water.

facts.question: A watermelon is over what percent water?
facts.reveal: Red, pink, orange, or yellow, a watermelon is mostly water.

sources.title: Watermelon | SNAP-Ed
sources.publisher: USDA Food and Nutrition Service, SNAP-Ed Connection (Seasonal Produce Guide)
sources.supports: A watermelon is over 90% water and comes in red, pink, orange, and yellow.

facts.question: About how many seeds sit on the outside of an average strawberry?
facts.reveal: Each tiny speck is really a small fruit with a seed inside.

sources.title: Strawberries | SNAP-Ed
sources.publisher: USDA Food and Nutrition Service, SNAP-Ed Connection (Seasonal Produce Guide)
sources.supports: Fun fact: an average strawberry has about 200 seeds on the outside.

sources.title: Digital Flowers: Fruits, Flower to fruit, Fragaria
sources.publisher: University of Illinois (life.illinois.edu)
sources.supports: The whole strawberry is an enlarged fleshy receptacle; the actual fruits are the tiny achenes scattered on its surface.

facts.question: Botanically, is a peanut a true nut or a legume?
facts.reveal: Peanuts do not meet the botanical definition of a true nut.

sources.title: Nuts (Celebrating Wildflowers, Ethnobotany: Food)
sources.publisher: USDA Forest Service
sources.supports: Peanuts are actually legumes and do not meet the botanical definition of a true nut.

facts.question: Botanically speaking, is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable?
facts.reveal: Cooks use it like a vegetable, but botanically it is a fruit.

sources.title: Tomatoes
sources.publisher: MU Extension, University of Missouri (2018-07-31)
sources.supports: Botanically speaking, tomatoes are more of a fruit; in cooking and nutrition they are considered a vegetable.

facts.question: On which continent were potatoes first domesticated?
facts.reveal: Potatoes began in the Andes mountains of South America.

sources.title: Potato
sources.publisher: International Potato Center (CIP)
sources.supports: The potato originated and was first domesticated in the Andes mountains of South America.

facts.question: Which grain is the main staple food for over half the world's people?
facts.reveal: USDA says rice is the primary staple food for more than half the world.

sources.title: Rice - Rice Sector at a Glance
sources.publisher: USDA Economic Research Service (page updated 2026-10-09)
sources.supports: Rice is the primary staple food for more than half the world's population.

facts.question: What colors were the first cultivated carrots?
facts.reveal: Orange carrots came along later, first reported in Europe.

sources.title: Simon: Carrot Facts
sources.publisher: USDA Agricultural Research Service (P.W. Simon, Vegetable Crops Research Unit, Madison WI; modified 2020-08-17)
sources.supports: Timeline: purple and yellow carrots spread from Afghanistan to the eastern Mediterranean by 900-1000 AD; an orange type was first reported in The Netherlands and adjoining regions.

facts.question: What inside a popcorn kernel turns to steam and makes it pop?
facts.reveal: Steam builds pressure inside the tough hull until the kernel bursts.

sources.title: Celebrate National Popcorn Day with locally grown Illinois popcorn
sources.publisher: Illinois Extension, University of Illinois (Nicole Flowers-Kimmerle, 2026-01-16)
sources.supports: Kernels hold about 14% water that turns to steam and builds pressure inside a tough hull until the pop.

sources.title: Growing popcorn in home gardens
sources.publisher: University of Minnesota Extension (reviewed 2026)
sources.supports: A small amount of moisture within the hard kernel turns to steam, causing the kernel to burst.

facts.question: Do avocados ripen on the tree, or only after they are picked?
facts.reveal: Florida extension experts say avocados do not ripen on the tree.

sources.title: CIR1034/MG213: Avocado Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
sources.publisher: UF/IFAS Extension, University of Florida (Crane, Balerdi, Maguire)
sources.supports: Avocado fruit does not generally ripen until it falls or is picked from the tree.

facts.question: Kale, cabbage, and broccoli were all bred from which one wild plant?
facts.reveal: Growers bred one plant into many vegetables, from leafy kale to flowering broccoli.

sources.title: We've been genetically altering plants for thousands of years
sources.publisher: Illinois Extension, University of Illinois (Christopher Enroth)
sources.supports: Wild cabbage (Brassica oleracea) was selectively bred into broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, kale, and more.

sources.title: Is Broccoli Man-Made?
sources.publisher: Cornell Cooperative Extension of Orange County NY (Joan Kean, 2022-01-28)
sources.supports: Broccoli is a derivative of Brassica oleracea; many Brassica vegetables are cultivars of one wild mustard/cabbage species.

facts.question: As a green bell pepper ripens, which colors can it turn?
facts.reveal: A pepper's color tells you how ripe it is.

sources.title: Bell Peppers | SNAP-Ed
sources.publisher: USDA Food and Nutrition Service, SNAP-Ed Connection (Seasonal Produce Guide)
sources.supports: The color of a pepper indicates its ripeness; as they ripen they change from green to yellow, orange, and eventually red.

sources.title: Peppers (Home Vegetable Gardening)
sources.publisher: Illinois Extension, University of Illinois
sources.supports: Bell peppers may be harvested green or left on the plant to ripen to red, yellow, orange, or brown.

facts.question: Pumpkins are native to which part of the world?
facts.reveal: Pumpkins have been grown in North America for thousands of years.

sources.title: Pumpkin: An ancient vegetable still in vogue today
sources.publisher: MU Extension, University of Missouri (2024-10-10)
sources.supports: Archaeological evidence suggests pumpkins and winter squash are native to the Americas; pumpkins have been grown in North America for about 5,000 years.

sources.title: The History of Squash
sources.publisher: Illinois Extension, University of Illinois (Ryan Pankau, 2017-11-22)
sources.supports: Squash and pumpkins originated in the New World (genus Cucurbita), with Mexico believed to be the point of origin of the genus.

facts.question: About how many blueberries can one bush produce in a year?
facts.reveal: A single blueberry bush can make more than 6,000 berries each year.

sources.title: Blueberries | SNAP-Ed
sources.publisher: USDA Food and Nutrition Service, SNAP-Ed Connection (Seasonal Produce Guide)
sources.supports: Fun fact: a single blueberry bush can produce over 6,000 blueberries each year.
